title: Four waters (Teresa, Life 11)
hook: watering a garden by bucket, wheel, stream and rain
tomorrow: what kind of fire wounds you and does no harm?

segments.voice: This week: Benedict's tools, Bernard's love with no scale, Anselm's longing, Hildegard's green, Francis's song with Sister Death in it, and Clare's four steps of looking. Yesterday's line: gaze.

A hose that breaks in a dry week means hauling water by hand, bucket after bucket, arms aching, the plants still looking thirsty. So how many ways are there to water a garden? Teresa of Avila counted four. She asks her readers to picture a soul beginning to pray as a garden on poor ground, full of weeds. The Lord pulls the weeds and plants good seed. The gardener's job is the watering, and that job changes as the garden grows.
screen: `THE HOSE BREAKS.` → `A GARDEN ON POOR GROUND.` → `THE GARDENER WATERS.`

segments.voice: First, the bucket. You haul water up from a well by hand, and it's heavy work. Teresa compares this to beginners in prayer: gathering a scattered mind, again and again, and some days the well seems dry. Second, the wheel, a water wheel with buckets, turned by a crank. More water, less sweat. Prayer here starts to get easier, in her picture; God is doing more of the lifting. In Teresa's Spanish the wheel is a noria, the kind farmers used to lift water out of a well. Third, the stream. A river or a spring runs right through the garden, and the gardener only has to guide it. Fourth, the rain. Nobody hauls anything. It simply falls and soaks everything, and the gardener does nothing but receive it. The image moves from almost all effort to almost all gift, and Teresa never pretends the first bucket is optional. She wrote her Life at the request of her confessors, and the garden keeps coming back in the chapters after this one. Today is only the map: bucket, wheel, stream, then rain.
screen: `THE BUCKET: HAULED BY HAND.` · `THE WHEEL: LESS SWEAT.` · `THE STREAM: ONLY GUIDED.` · `THE RAIN: SIMPLY RECEIVED.` · then, large: `THEN RAIN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice what your prayer, or your quiet time, feels like right now: a bucket hauled up hard, a wheel turning a little easier, a stream, or rain. Don't judge it; only name it. If you pray, offer the garden as it is.
Four waters. Teresa's picture of prayer as watering a garden: bucket, wheel, stream, rain.
Pocket this one: then rain, the water nobody has to haul, falling on a garden someone kept watering by hand. That's the week.

fork.reveal: Teresa compares beginners to hauling water by hand, some days from a dry well. the image moves toward gift, but she never calls the first bucket optional.

chat.says: hose broke, so i watered abuela's garden by bucket all week. last night it poured. still waitlisted. now what?
options: Keep your buckets going. For Teresa, rain is gift: you don't haul it, you're ready for it.
Stop watering. If rain comes anyway, the bucket work never mattered much.
Haul harder. Teresa says enough buckets will finally make the rain come.
chat.meaning: Teresa's four waters move from effort to gift: bucket, wheel, stream, then rain that simply falls. She never calls the first bucket optional.
